title: TrajCFG: Token-Wise Classifier-Free Guidancevia Denoising Trajectory Feedback

paper.title: TrajCFG: Token-Wise Classifier-Free Guidance via Denoising Trajectory Feedback
paper.abstract:
Abstract Classifier-free guidance (CFG) typically applies a shared scale to all
latent tokens, although their velocity predictions evolve differently
during sampling. We introduce Trajectory-Adaptive Classifier-Free
Guidance (TrajCFG), a training-free method for flow-matching models
that adapts token-wise guidance using historical changes in guided
velocity direction. TrajCFG maps this feedback to bounded scales,
assigning stronger guidance to larger directional changes and weaker
guidance to more consistent directions. It combines adjacent-step
and interval-normalized longer-span feedback, reusing standard CFG
predictions without additional model evaluations. Controlled diagnostics
and ablations examine the roles of directional feedback, token-wise
allocation, and history-span fusion. Experiments on
text-to-video, image-to-video, text-to-audio-video, text-to-image,
and image-to-3D generation show improvements over base samplers
across multiple backbones. For text-to-video generation, TrajCFG
improves VBench Total scores by 0.30–0.75 points over the strongest
evaluated baseline on each of three backbones. These results support
historical directional feedback as a broadly applicable signal for
fine-grained guidance allocation. The project page is available at https://jyliu-98.github.io/trajcfg-project-page/ .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) provides a common framework for generative modeling by learning velocity fields that transport noise into data. Its applications span image, video, audiovisual, and 3D generation. Across these tasks, classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) steers generation toward desired conditions by combining target- and reference-conditioned predictions. Standard CFG typically applies a shared guidance scale to all latent sites at a given sampling step. Such uniform guidance does not account for differences in how local predictions evolve along the sampling trajectory, motivating adaptation to local sampling behavior. Recent work has improved CFG by adapting when and how guidance is applied. Guidance schedules vary its strength across noise levels ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , while spatially adaptive and velocity-based methods determine the scale from local guidance energy or within-step velocity alignment ( Li et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . Other approaches modify the guided update through optimized scaling or feedback corrections ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Inference-time refinement also uses a pretrained generator’s own predictions to improve samples through additional sampling operations ( Jang et al., 2026 ) . These developments raise a natural question: can directional changes in guided velocities already computed during sampling provide feedback for adapting CFG at each latent site? Our starting point is that guided velocity history records how the sampler revises its local predictions. Under Euler sampling, changes in guided velocity correspond to revisions of the sampler’s clean-endpoint estimate. Separating changes in direction from changes in magnitude provides a normalized directional statistic. Video visualizations show that historical velocity angles can exhibit content-related spatial structure. A controlled local reconstruction diagnostic further shows that reducing guidance tends to benefit sites with small historical angles, whereas increasing guidance tends to benefit those with larger angles. Together, these observations motivate guidance allocation based on historical directional changes. We evaluate the effectiveness of this principle across modalities through generation experiments. Figure 1: Overview of TrajCFG. Standard CFG uses a fixed scale (purple), while TrajCFG (teal) adapts each token’s scale using guided velocities from the two most recent completed steps. Larger historical angles yield stronger guidance; smaller angles yield weaker guidance. Predictions are reused without extra model evaluations. For clarity, the illustration shows adjacent-step feedback. Trajectories are schematic. We introduce Trajectory-Adaptive Classifier-Free Guidance (TrajCFG) , a training-free method for token-wise guidance adaptation in flow matching models. As illustrated in Figure 1 , TrajCFG compares guided velocities from the two most recent completed steps at each latent site and maps their cosine similarity to a bounded guidance scale. Larger directional changes receive stronger guidance, while more consistent directions receive weaker guidance. We use these scales to combine the current target- and reference-conditioned predictions. The guided velocities are then supplied to the solver and retained for subsequent steps, forming a feedback loop in which past sampling behavior informs future conditioning strength. We also incorporate interval-normalized longer-span feedback to complement the adjacent-step signal. Because the rule uses only local guided velocity histories and existing CFG predictions, it applies across modalities with different latent representations. TrajCFG requires neither auxiliary networks nor extra model evaluations and leaves the pretrained model and sampling solver unchanged. We evaluate TrajCFG across text-to-video, image-to-video, text-to-audio-video, text-to-image, and image-to-3D generation. Experiments show improvements in generation quality and conditional alignment across diverse model families. Controlled diagnostics and ablation studies examine the roles of token-wise allocation, historical directional feedback, and the combination of history spans. Together, these results support TrajCFG as a broadly applicable approach to adaptive CFG in flow matching models.

sections.heading: Scheduling and adaptive classifier-free guidance.
sections.text: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines target- and reference-conditioned predictions to control generation ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . Guidance schedules and limited-interval guidance vary conditioning strength with noise level ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) , while Adaptive Guidance and Step AG selectively omit guidance evaluations ( Castillo et al., 2025 ; Zhang and Wan, 2025 ) . C 2 C^{2} FG and stage-wise analyses motivate time-dependent scales through score discrepancies and sampling dynamics, respectively ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2026 ) . Online-feedback CFG selects scales using trained latent-space evaluators ( Papalampidi et al., 2026 ) , whereas PathGuide uses on-policy transport alignment for online scale adaptation or offline schedule fitting ( Nevo and Hazan, 2026 ) . TrajCFG extends adaptation to token-wise scales driven by cross-step changes in guided velocity direction.

sections.heading: Geometry-, spatial-, and history-aware guidance.
sections.text: CFG++, APG, and TCFG modify guidance through manifold constraints, projection and momentum, and score-component filtering, respectively ( Chung et al., 2025 ; Sadat et al., 2024 ; Kwon et al., 2025 ) . CFG-Zero combines within-step projection with suppression of initial updates ( Fan et al., 2025 ) , while VAGS adjusts a sample-wise scale using sampling progress and conditional–unconditional velocity alignment ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . For spatial adaptation, S-CFG uses attention-based semantic regions ( Shen et al., 2024 ) , whereas SAMG derives point-wise scales from current-step guidance difference energy ( Li et al., 2026 ) . History informs APG’s momentum, CFG-Ctrl’s discrepancy-based feedback correction ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , and HiGS’s additional direction from current and aggregated past denoised predictions ( Sadat et al., 2026 ) . TrajCFG instead measures cross-step angular changes of the guided velocity at each fixed latent site to set bounded token-wise CFG scales for the next step. The feedback is computed from guided velocities at completed sampling steps and modulates the current target–reference prediction difference without introducing a separate update direction. sections.heading: Inference-time refinement and sampling interventions.
sections.text: Beyond CFG adaptation, FreeInit refines low-frequency initial noise ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , while Restart and Zigzag Sampling introduce additional noising–denoising or inversion operations ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . VideoGuide uses additional teacher or self-guided steps ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , and Self-Refining Video Sampling performs fixed-noise predict-and-perturb refinement ( Jang et al., 2026 ) . FlowMo optimizes latents with a motion objective ( Shaulov et al., 2026 ) , whereas SpecLoR spectrally corrects a clean-latent lookahead ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . PAG and STG construct weak predictions through attention perturbation and layer skipping ( Ahn et al., 2024 ; Hyung et al., 2025 ) ; STAS intervenes on sparse massive network activations ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . TrajCFG uses a short history of velocities already computed during standard CFG sampling, requiring no auxiliary evaluator, extra model evaluations, latent optimization, or model-internal changes.

sections.text: Flow Matching. Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) learns a velocity field that continuously transforms noise into data. During generation, a numerical solver integrates the learned field from τ = 1 \tau=1 to τ = 0 \tau=0 , starting from noise. Classifier-Free Guidance. At sampling step k k , given the latent 𝐳 k \mathbf{z}_{k} and time τ k \tau_{k} , a pretrained model predicts velocities under target conditioning y + y^{+} and reference conditioning y − y^{-} : 𝐯 k + = f θ ​ ( 𝐳 k , τ k , y + ) , 𝐯 k − = f θ ​ ( 𝐳 k , τ k , y − ) . \mathbf{v}_{k}^{+}=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{k},\tau_{k};y^{+}),\qquad\mathbf{v}_{k}^{-}=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{k},\tau_{k};y^{-}). sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: TrajCFG adapts the guidance scale at each latent site using historical changes in guided velocity direction. We first motivate this feedback signal, then define the token-wise allocation rule and its extension to longer history spans.

sections.heading: 4.1 Motivation: Directional Changes as Guidance Feedback

These findings motivate us to investigate whether the directional evolution of guided velocities provides useful feedback for allocating guidance across latent sites. Figure 2 illustrates historical velocity angles in two video examples. Larger angles concentrate around the foreground subjects, while much of the background exhibits smaller angles. This content-related structure suggests that guided velocity history captures differences in local sampling behavior. The statistic itself depends only on velocity histories at individual latent sites and can be computed across modalities. These observations motivate a simple allocation principle: assign weaker guidance to sites with more consistent historical directions and stronger guidance to those with larger directional revisions. Its use in generation rests on the hypothesis that the association observed in the controlled reconstruction diagnostic remains informative along actual sampling trajectories. The following subsection implements this principle through a bounded mapping from historical directional feedback to token-wise guidance scales. We evaluate its effectiveness across generative modalities and examine its components through ablation studies.

Each site corresponds to a token indexed by p p , whose velocity is a C C -dimensional vector. Depending on the backbone, the site axis may represent spatial, temporal, spatiotemporal, or generic sequence positions. sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We compare TrajCFG with inference-time enhancement methods for text-to-video and image-to-video generation, ablate its guidance allocation rule, and evaluate three additional generation tasks.

sections.heading: 5.1 Benchmarks
sections.text: For T2V, we use VBench ( Huang et al., 2024 ) and Dynamic-Bench ( Jang et al., 2026 ) ; for I2V, we use VBench-I2V ( Huang et al., 2025 ) and PAI-Bench-G ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . We follow the official protocols for VBench and VBench-I2V. Dynamic-Bench and PAI-Bench-G use the supported dimensions under the VBench custom evaluation protocol; these scores are distinct from the official aggregate scores.

sections.heading: 5.2 Backbones and Baselines
sections.text: For T2V, we evaluate Wan2.1-1.3B, Wan2.2-5B, and Wan2.2-14B ( Wan et al., 2025 ) ; for I2V, we use Cosmos-Predict2.5-2B ( Ali et al., 2025 ) and both Wan2.2 backbones. We compare with the original sampling configuration ( Base ) and four training-free methods: CFG-Zero ( Fan et al., 2025 ) , CFG-Ctrl ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , PAG ( Ahn et al., 2024 ) , and Self-Refining Video Sampling (SRVS) ( Jang et al., 2026 ) . TrajCFG is labeled Ours in figures; guidance hyperparameters and step counts appear in Appendix Table 7 .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced TrajCFG, a training-free method that adapts token-wise CFG scales using historical changes in guided velocity direction. By combining adjacent-step and interval-normalized longer-span feedback, TrajCFG allocates guidance from sampling history without additional model evaluations. Experiments show improvements across video backbones and applicability to audiovisual, image, and 3D generation. These results support historical directional feedback as a useful signal for local guidance allocation across latent representations. Historical directional feedback tracks revisions of the sampler’s predictions rather than directly estimating generation error. Its effectiveness beyond the evaluated models and sampling configurations remains to be established, particularly for very low-step sampling and alternative generative parameterizations. Future work could investigate self-calibrating guidance rules that reduce manual parameter selection without additional training or model evaluations.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.14153v1 [cs.CV] 09 Oct 2026 TrajCFG: Token-Wise Classifier-Free Guidance via Denoising Trajectory Feedback Jingyu Liu Hao Jiang Yikang Ding Huafeng Shi Affiliation: Kling Team, Kuaishou Technology Xu Yang Affiliation: Kling Team, Kuaishou Technology Xiaoqiang Liu Affiliation: Kling Team, Kuaishou Technology Guoxin Zhang Affiliation: Kling Team, Kuaishou Technology Pengfei Wan Affiliation: Kling Team, Kuaishou Technology Kun Gai Affiliation: Renmin University of China Abstract Classifier-free guidance (CFG) typically applies a shared scale to all latent tokens, although their velocity predictions evolve differently during sampling. We introduce Trajectory-Adaptive Classifier-Free Guidance (TrajCFG), a training-free method for flow-matching models that adapts token-wise guidance using historical changes in guided velocity direction. TrajCFG maps this feedback to bounded scales, assigning stronger guidance to larger directional changes and weaker guidance to more consistent directions. It combines adjacent-step and interval-normalized longer-span feedback, reusing standard CFG predictions without additional model evaluations. Controlled diagnostics and ablations examine the roles of directional feedback, token-wise allocation, and history-span fusion. Experiments on text-to-video, image-to-video, text-to-audio-video, text-to-image, and image-to-3D generation show improvements over base samplers across multiple backbones. For text-to-video generation, TrajCFG improves VBench Total scores by 0.30–0.75 points over the strongest evaluated baseline on each of three backbones. These results support historical directional feedback as a broadly applicable signal for fine-grained guidance allocation. The project page is available at https://jyliu-98.github.io/trajcfg-project-page/ . 2 2 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 4 4 footnotetext: Work done at Kling Team, Kuaishou Technology. 3 3 footnotetext: Project Leader. 1 1 footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) provides a common framework for generative modeling by learning velocity fields that transport noise into data. Its applications span image, video, audiovisual, and 3D generation. Across these tasks, classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) steers generation toward desired conditions by combining target- and reference-conditioned predictions. Standard CFG typically applies a shared guidance scale to all latent sites at a given sampling step. Such uniform guidance does not account for differences in how local predictions evolve along the sampling trajectory, motivating adaptation to local sampling behavior. Recent work has improved CFG by adapting when and how guidance is applied. Guidance schedules vary its strength across noise levels ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , while spatially adaptive and velocity-based methods determine the scale from local guidance energy or within-step velocity alignment ( Li et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . Other approaches modify the guided update through optimized scaling or feedback corrections ( Fan et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Inference-time refinement also uses a pretrained generator’s own predictions to improve samples through additional sampling operations ( Jang et al., 2026 ) . These developments raise a natural question: can directional changes in guided velocities already computed during sampling provide feedback for adapting CFG at each latent site? Our starting point is that guided velocity history records how the sampler revises its local predictions. Under Euler sampling, changes in guided velocity correspond to revisions of the sampler’s clean-endpoint estimate. Separating changes in direction from changes in magnitude provides a normalized directional statistic. Video visualizations show that historical velocity angles can exhibit content-related spatial structure. A controlled local reconstruction diagnostic further shows that reducing guidance tends to benefit sites with small historical angles, whereas increasing guidance tends to benefit those with larger angles. Together, these observations motivate guidance allocation based on historical directional changes. We evaluate the effectiveness of this principle across modalities through generation experiments. Figure 1: Overview of TrajCFG. Standard CFG uses a fixed scale (purple), while TrajCFG (teal) adapts each token’s scale using guided velocities from the two most recent completed steps. Larger historical angles yield stronger guidance; smaller angles yield weaker guidance. Predictions are reused without extra model evaluations. For clarity, the illustration shows adjacent-step feedback. Trajectories are schematic. We introduce Trajectory-Adaptive Classifier-Free Guidance (TrajCFG) , a training-free method for token-wise guidance adaptation in flow matching models. As illustrated in Figure 1 , TrajCFG compares guided velocities from the two most recent completed steps at each latent site and maps their cosine similarity to a bounded guidance scale. Larger directional changes receive stronger guidance, while more consistent directions receive weaker guidance. We use these scales to combine the current target- and reference-conditioned predictions. The guided velocities are then supplied to the solver and retained for subsequent steps, forming a feedback loop in which past sampling behavior informs future conditioning strength. We also incorporate interval-normalized longer-span feedback to complement the adjacent-step signal. Because the rule uses only local guided velocity histories and existing CFG predictions, it applies across modalities with different latent representations. TrajCFG requires neither auxiliary networks nor extra model evaluations and leaves the pretrained model and sampling solver unchanged. We evaluate TrajCFG across text-to-video, image-to-video, text-to-audio-video, text-to-image, and image-to-3D generation. Experiments show improvements in generation quality and conditional alignment across diverse model families. Controlled diagnostics and ablation studies examine the roles of token-wise allocation, historical directional feedback, and the combination of history spans. Together, these results support TrajCFG as a broadly applicable approach to adaptive CFG in flow matching models. 2 Related Work Scheduling and adaptive classifier-free guidance. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines target- and reference-conditioned predictions to control generation ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . Guidance schedules and limited-interval guidance vary conditioning strength with noise level ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) , while Adaptive Guidance and Step AG selectively omit guidance evaluations ( Castillo et al., 2025 ; Zhang and Wan, 2025 ) . C 2 C^{2} FG and stage-wise analyses motivate time-dependent scales through score discrepancies and sampling dynamics, respectively ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2026 ) . Online-feedback CFG selects scales using trained latent-space evaluators ( Papalampidi et al., 2026 ) , whereas PathGuide uses on-policy transport alignment for online scale adaptation or offline schedule fitting ( Nevo and Hazan, 2026 ) . TrajCFG extends adaptation to token-wise scales driven by cross-step changes in guided velocity direction. Geometry-, spatial-, and history-aware guidance. CFG++, APG, and TCFG modify guidance through manifold constraints, projection and momentum, and score-component filtering, respectively ( Chung et al., 2025 ; Sadat et al., 2024 ; Kwon et al., 2025 ) . CFG-Zero combines within-step projection with suppression of initial updates ( Fan et al., 2025 ) , while VAGS adjusts a sample-wise scale using sampling progress and conditional–unconditional velocity alignment ( Luo et al., 2026 ) . For spatial adaptation, S-CFG uses attention-based semantic regions ( Shen et al., 2024 ) , whereas SAMG derives point-wise scales from current-step guidance difference energy ( Li et al., 2026 ) . History informs APG’s momentum, CFG-Ctrl’s discrepancy-based feedback correction ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , and HiGS’s additional direction from current and aggregated past denoised predictions ( Sadat et al., 2026 ) . TrajCFG instead measures cross-step angular changes of the guided velocity at each fixed latent site to set bounded token-wise CFG scales for the next step. The feedback is computed from guided velocities at completed sampling steps and modulates the current target–reference prediction difference without introducing a separate update direction. Warmer colors indicate larger angular changes. Inference-time refinement and sampling interventions. Beyond CFG adaptation, FreeInit refines low-frequency initial noise ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , while Restart and Zigzag Sampling introduce additional noising–denoising or inversion operations ( Xu et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . VideoGuide uses additional teacher or self-guided steps ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , and Self-Refining Video Sampling performs fixed-noise predict-and-perturb refinement ( Jang et al., 2026 ) . FlowMo optimizes latents with a motion objective ( Shaulov et al., 2026 ) , whereas SpecLoR spectrally corrects a clean-latent lookahead ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . PAG and STG construct weak predictions through attention perturbation and layer skipping ( Ahn et al., 2024 ; Hyung et al., 2025 ) ; STAS intervenes on sparse massive network activations ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . TrajCFG uses a short history of velocities already computed during standard CFG sampling, requiring no auxiliary evaluator, extra model evaluations, latent optimization, or model-internal changes. 3 Preliminaries Flow Matching. Flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) learns a velocity field that continuously transforms noise into data. Under an affine path formulation, the interpolation between a clean data latent 𝐱 \mathbf{x} and noise ϵ \bm{\epsilon} is 𝐳 τ = ( 1 − τ ) ​ 𝐱 + τ ​ ϵ , τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \mathbf{z}_{\tau}=(1-\tau)\mathbf{x}+\tau\bm{\epsilon},\qquad\tau\in[0,1], (1) with path velocity ϵ − 𝐱 \bm{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x} . At sampling step k k , given the latent 𝐳 k \mathbf{z}_{k} and time τ k \tau_{k} , a pretrained model predicts velocities under target conditioning y + y^{+} and reference conditioning y − y^{-} : 𝐯 k + = f θ ​ ( 𝐳 k , τ k , y + ) , 𝐯 k − = f θ ​ ( 𝐳 k , τ k , y − ) . \mathbf{v}_{k}^{+}=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{k},\tau_{k};y^{+}),\qquad\mathbf{v}_{k}^{-}=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{k},\tau_{k};y^{-}). (3) The sampling solver then updates the latent using the guided velocity 𝐯 ^ k \widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{k} . We use latent site to denote a position in the latent representation and token to denote its channel vector; a token-wise guidance scale is shared across that vector’s channels. 4 Method TrajCFG adapts the guidance scale at each latent site using historical changes in guided velocity direction. We first motivate this feedback signal, then define the token-wise allocation rule and its extension to longer history spans. 4.1 Motivation: Directional Changes as Guidance Feedback Standard CFG in Eq. ( 3 ) applies a shared guidance scale s base s_{\mathrm{base}} across all latent sites, even though their velocity predictions may evolve differently during sampling. Prior work shows that guidance utility varies across noise levels ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) and that local prediction statistics can inform adaptive guidance ( Li et al., 2026 ) . These findings motivate us to investigate whether the directional evolution of guided velocities provides useful feedback for allocating guidance across latent sites. Figure 2 illustrates historical velocity angles in two video examples. Larger angles concentrate around the foreground subjects, while much of the background exhibits smaller angles. This content-related structure suggests that guided velocity history captures differences in local sampling behavior. The statistic itself depends only on velocity histories at individual latent sites and can be computed across modalities. We next examine what directional changes represent and whether they inform local guidance benefits. Interpreting directional changes. These observations motivate a simple allocation principle: assign weaker guidance to sites with more consistent historical directions and stronger guidance to those with larger directional revisions. Its use in generation rests on the hypothesis that the association observed in the controlled reconstruction diagnostic remains informative along actual sampling trajectories. The following subsection implements this principle through a bounded mapping from historical directional feedback to token-wise guidance scales. We evaluate its effectiveness across generative modalities and examine its components through ablation studies. 4.2 Token-Wise Guidance from Trajectory Feedback Following the allocation principle above, TrajCFG uses historical directional changes to determine the guidance scale at each latent site. Let 𝐳 k ∈ ℝ P × C \mathbf{z}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{P\times C} denote the latent at sampling step k k , where P P is the number of sites and C C is the number of channels; we omit the batch dimension. Each site corresponds to a token indexed by p p , whose velocity is a C C -dimensional vector. By combining adjacent-step and interval-normalized longer-span feedback, TrajCFG allocates guidance from sampling history without additional model evaluations. Experiments show improvements across video backbones and applicability to audiovisual, image, and 3D generation. These results support historical directional feedback as a useful signal for local guidance allocation across latent representations. Historical directional feedback tracks revisions of the sampler’s predictions rather than directly estimating generation error. Its effectiveness beyond the evaluated models and sampling configurations remains to be established, particularly for very low-step sampling and alternative generative parameterizations. Future work could investigate self-calibrating guidance rules that reduce manual parameter selection without additional training or model evaluations. Appendix Contents A Additional Method Details .
